content: Medications or mechanical dilators are frequently employed to soften and dilate the cervix before performing a surgical evacuation of the uterus in cases of non-viable pregnancy or miscarriage. Most miscarriages occur during the first trimester. The purpose of cervical ripening is to minimize the risk of injury to the uterus and cervix while facilitating the surgical procedure. However, cervical ripening agents can cause adverse effects, and it remains uncertain whether the benefits of their use outweigh the associated risks. The objective of this review was to systematically evaluate the benefits and harms of using cervical ripening agents prior to surgical evacuation of non-viable pregnancies occurring before 14 weeks of gestation. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies up to April 30, 2015. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the use of pharmacological or mechanical agents for cervical ripening in women undergoing dilation and curettage (D&C) or vacuum aspiration for non-viable pregnancies before 14 weeks of gestation. Cluster-randomized trials and cross-over design trials were excluded. Although unpublished RCTs and quasi-randomized trials were eligible, none were identified. Nine trials involving 469 women were included in the review. These trials investigated a variety of medications and regimens, which limited the ability to perform meta-analyses. Data from six trials with 383 participants were used for comparisons, but the trials were small and had unclear risks of bias. Three trials met inclusion criteria but did not provide usable data. The review conducted four comparisons: isosorbide mononitrate or dinitrate versus misoprostol, misoprostol versus placebo, chemical dilation versus mechanical dilation, and any cervical preparation versus placebo. None of the included studies reported on the primary outcome of cervical or uterine injury, such as perforation, laceration, or creation of a false passage. There was no clear difference between isosorbide compounds and misoprostol in terms of the need for manual cervical dilation (average risk ratio [RR] 0.76, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.10 to 5.64; three trials, 150 women). However, the data were heterogeneous. Misoprostol was associated with more vomiting compared to isosorbide compounds (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.85; two trials, 120 women), but there were no significant differences in other adverse effects, such as headache, nausea, or hypotension. The dosing regimens varied across trials in terms of dose, frequency, and route of administration. In a single trial involving 65 women, mechanical dilators (Dilapan-S hygroscopic dilators) performed similarly to chemical dilators in terms of difficulty in cervical dilation, excessive bleeding, and adverse effects. Misoprostol was found to be more effective than placebo for cervical ripening, as it reduced the need for manual cervical dilation (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.26; one trial, 120 women) and shortened surgical time (mean difference [MD] -3.15 minutes, 95% CI -3.59 to -2.70; one trial, 120 women). However, misoprostol was associated with more abdominal pain compared to placebo (RR 29.00, 95% CI 1.77 to 475.35; one trial, 120 women). No significant differences in other adverse effects, such as nausea, vomiting, headache, or fever, were observed between misoprostol and placebo. When comparing chemical dilation to mechanical dilators, no significant differences were observed in outcomes such as difficulty in cervical dilation, excessive bleeding, or adverse effects. Compared to placebo, any cervical preparation reduced the need for manual cervical dilation (average RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.89; two trials, 168 women) and shortened surgical time (MD -2.55 minutes, 95% CI -3.67 to -1.43; two trials, 168 women). None of the included trials reported on secondary outcomes such as injury to the bladder or bowel, miscarriage or preterm birth in subsequent pregnancies, analgesia use before or after surgery, or satisfaction with the procedure. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to determine whether cervical ripening before first-trimester surgical evacuation reduces the rate of cervical or uterine injury, likely because these outcomes are rare. Cervical preparation was shown to reduce the need for manual cervical dilation compared to placebo. Misoprostol and isosorbide mononitrate or dinitrate were similarly effective for cervical ripening, although misoprostol was associated with more vomiting. Mechanical dilators performed comparably to chemical dilators. However, the included studies were small, and their methodological quality was mixed, limiting the reliability of the conclusions. Larger, high-quality trials are needed to assess the benefits and risks of cervical ripening agents, including their impact on rare outcomes such as cervical or uterine injury. Future research should also evaluate women's satisfaction, outcomes in subsequent pregnancies, and whether the benefits of reduced manual cervical dilation outweigh the risks of adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting, headache, fever, diarrhea, and pain.
